title: Vocabulary: topic collocations for common IELTS themes
status: Owner approved v1.1.0 on 2026-10-26; teacher release to all eligible schools (optional vocabulary lesson)
rights: Original Brains Heist LLC instructional material, AI-assisted. Passages, people and data are fictional and created for practice. Not official IELTS material. Human editorial and classroom review recommended.
prerequisites: Lesson 15 (Task 2 under time) or Lesson 16 (Speaking Part 3).
Learners have written at least one Task 2 essay and taken part in a Part 3 discussion.
Pitched at learners aiming for Band 6.5-7.5; use V1 first with learners who still struggle with paraphrase.

objectives.text: Use 14 precise collocations for frequent IELTS themes (environment, health, education, work, technology, cities) with the correct verb, preposition and grammar.
Recognise the same ideas when an IELTS passage expresses them in different words.
Develop Part 3 answers with reasons, examples and qualifications, using topic vocabulary only where it fits naturally.

levels.foundation: Use the word bank during the multiple-choice task; in the discussion, answer with a reason and one example.
levels.core: Complete all tasks with the word bank closed after the first stage; extend each Part 3 answer after a follow-up question.
levels.extension: In the discussion, qualify at least one claim (for example 'in most cases', 'not necessarily') and explain the exception.
levels.high_band: In the homework paragraph, concede one counter-argument and rebut it, with every collocation used accurately and naturally.

word_bank.meaning: reduce the gases that cause global warming
word_bank.example: Low-traffic zones are one way to curb carbon emissions.

word_bank.meaning: destruction of the places where wild animals live / a species at risk of extinction
word_bank.example: Habitat loss is the main threat to many endangered species.

word_bank.meaning: a way of life with little physical activity
word_bank.example: Office work can lead to a sedentary lifestyle.

word_bank.item: place / put a strain on (health services)
word_bank.meaning: create pressure that is difficult to manage
word_bank.example: An ageing population places a strain on hospitals.

word_bank.meaning: gain abilities that are useful in many jobs
word_bank.example: Volunteering helps students acquire transferable skills.

word_bank.meaning: encourage the ability to question and evaluate
work with no security (short contracts, no guaranteed hours)
word_bank.example: Precarious employment makes it hard to plan for the future.

word_bank.item: strike a balance between A and B
word_bank.meaning: give the right amount of attention to two things
word_bank.example: Remote work can help people strike a balance between career and family.

word_bank.meaning: make people worried about personal information

word_bank.example: Streaming has rendered DVDs largely obsolete.
Better bus services could alleviate traffic congestion.

word_bank.meaning: uncontrolled spread of a city / homes ordinary people can pay for
make a problem worse / make its effects less serious
word_bank.example: Heatwaves exacerbate air pollution; trees can mitigate it.

word_bank.meaning: affect many people or areas strongly
word_bank.example: Planning decisions have far-reaching consequences for health.

stages.title: Opening challenge: accurate, wrong or forced?
stages.student: Decide which answer an examiner would reward most, and why the others lose credit.
stages.teacher: Learners vote. Reveal the comments. Stress that forced vocabulary is penalised as much as wrong vocabulary.
stages.say: Use a collocation when it says exactly what you mean, not to show that you know it.
stages.check: Learners can name one problem with Answer A and one with Answer C.

stages.title: Word bank: collocations in context
stages.student: With a partner, cover the meaning column and explain each item in your own words; then check.
stages.teacher: Drill stress: SED-en-ta-ry, pre-CAR-i-ous, ex-AC-er-bate, al-LE-vi-ate. Point out the grammar: place a strain ON, strike a balance BETWEEN, render something obsolete.
stages.say: Learn the verb, the noun and the preposition together.
stages.check: Each pair explains ten items without the meaning column.

stages.title: Which word fits exactly?
stages.student: Choose the one option that is natural and correct. All the options are real English words.
stages.teacher: Six minutes, word bank closed for core and above. During the reveal, ask why each wrong option fails: meaning, grammar or collocation.
stages.say: Every option is a real word. Check meaning, grammar and the word it goes with.
stages.check: Learners explain the reason a distractor fails for at least four questions.

stages.title: Reading: the fifteen-minute city
stages.student: Answer the ten questions in twelve minutes. Underline the words in the passage that express the same idea as each question.
stages.teacher: Twelve minutes, then a two-minute reveal. For each answer, ask learners to read out the paraphrase that decided it.
stages.say: The questions use different words from the passage; match the idea, then check every detail.
stages.check: Learners quote evidence for each answer, including why Question 3 is NOT GIVEN.

stages.title: Speaking Part 3: interactive discussion
stages.student: Take turns as examiner and candidate. The examiner asks a question and then follows up; the candidate develops each answer.
stages.teacher: About six minutes per role, then swap. Circulate and note one well-developed answer and one place where a precise collocation would have helped.
stages.say: Answer, explain, give an example, then qualify. Topic words should help you say more, not replace thinking.
stages.check: Each candidate gives at least two answers extended by a follow-up.

stages.title: Compare with the model discussion
stages.student: Read the model exchange. Mark where the candidate gives a reason, an example and a qualification.
stages.teacher: Read the model aloud with a learner. Point out that the collocations appear only where they are needed.
stages.say: The model is illustrative, not a target band or a script to memorise.
stages.check: Learners identify the qualification in the second answer.

stages.title: Exit ticket and homework
stages.student: Complete the exit ticket and note the two homework tasks.
stages.teacher: Collect the exit tickets. Explain that the paragraph will be checked against the four criteria.
stages.say: Use the paragraph to show control, not quantity.
stages.check: Every learner writes two accurate collocations from memory.

blocks.title: Accurate, wrong or forced?
blocks.mode: Opening challenge; learners decide before the reveal
blocks.instructions: Examiner (Part 3): 'Why do you think so many people today do not get enough exercise?' Three candidates began their answers like this. Which opening would an examiner reward most?

examples.label: Answer A
examples.text: Because many people do a sitting life and make too much screen time.
examples.comment: Inaccurate: the collocations are 'lead a sedentary lifestyle' and 'spend too much time on screens'. The idea is fine; the vocabulary hides it.

examples.label: Answer B
examples.text: I think it's largely because so many jobs are desk-based now, so people end up with a fairly sedentary lifestyle unless they make a real effort to exercise.
examples.comment: Best: one precise collocation, a clear cause and a natural qualification ('largely', 'unless').

examples.label: Answer C
examples.text: A sedentary lifestyle exacerbates and mitigates far-reaching consequences, placing a strain on endangered species.
examples.comment: Forced: the phrases are real but do not belong together, and 'exacerbates and mitigates' contradicts itself. Examiners penalise vocabulary that is used without control.

blocks.title: Which word fits exactly?
blocks.mode: Controlled practice; word bank closed for core and above
blocks.instructions: Choose the correct option, A, B, C or D, to complete each sentence. All the options are real English words; only one is natural and grammatically correct in this sentence.

items.prompt: Many governments have introduced low-traffic zones in an attempt to ______ carbon emissions.
items.evidence: curb carbon emissions (transitive verb + object)
items.reason: Fall, decline and descend cannot take an object: emissions fall, but you cannot 'fall emissions'.

items.prompt: Long hours at a desk and little exercise often lead to a ______ lifestyle.
items.evidence: a sedentary lifestyle = a way of life with little physical activity
items.reason: 'Motionless' means not moving at a particular moment; a 'settled' lifestyle means living in one place or a calm routine; a 'stagnant' life is one that is not developing. None of them means 'inactive'.

items.prompt: The rapid growth in the number of elderly patients is ______ a strain on hospitals.
items.evidence: place / put a strain on
items.reason: 'Make', 'do' and 'give' do not collocate with 'a strain on'.

items.prompt: Part-time jobs allow students to ______ transferable skills such as teamwork and time management.
items.evidence: acquire skills
items.reason: You do not 'win', 'earn' or 'perform' a skill; 'perform' takes a task, not a skill.

items.prompt: Many young graduates face ______ employment, with short contracts and no guaranteed hours.
items.evidence: precarious employment = insecure work
items.reason: 'Dangerous' and 'hazardous' describe physical danger, which does not fit 'short contracts'; 'doubtful' does not collocate with employment.

items.prompt: Working from home can help parents ______ a balance between their careers and family life.
items.evidence: strike a balance between
items.reason: The fixed collocation is 'strike a balance'; 'set', 'beat' and 'take' are not used with 'a balance between'.

items.prompt: The use of facial recognition cameras in shopping centres has ______ serious privacy concerns.
items.evidence: raise concerns (transitive)
items.reason: 'Risen', 'arisen' and 'grown' are intransitive here: concerns rise or arise, but you cannot 'arise concerns'.

items.prompt: Building wider roads may actually ______ congestion, because it encourages more people to drive.
items.evidence: exacerbate = make worse (the sentence describes a worsening)
items.reason: 'Alleviate', 'mitigate' and 'relieve' all mean make less serious, the opposite of what the sentence describes.

blocks.title: Reading: the fifteen-minute city
blocks.mode: Timed practice under test-like conditions: twelve minutes, no dictionary
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-5: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN. Question 10: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D. Questions 6-9: Complete the summary sentences with words from the box. Write the correct letter. Four letters are not used. List of words: A suburbs; B regulations; C rents; D wealthier; E poorer; F villages; G salaries; H roads

stimulus.title: The fifteen-minute city
paragraphs: In recent years, urban planners in a number of European and North American cities have promoted the idea of the 'fifteen-minute city', a model in which residents can reach most of what they need in daily life, including work, schools, shops, health services and green space, within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle. Rather than concentrating offices in a central business district and housing on the periphery, the model encourages a mixture of uses within each neighbourhood, so that fewer journeys require a car.

Advocates present the idea as a response to several problems at once. Shorter journeys, they argue, would curb carbon emissions from transport and alleviate traffic congestion, although even enthusiastic supporters concede that congestion is unlikely to disappear altogether, since deliveries, emergency services and longer trips would still depend on roads. The model is also promoted as a means of improving public health: if walking or cycling becomes the most convenient way to reach a school or a pharmacy, physical activity is built into daily routines rather than reserved for leisure time, which may help to counter the effects of an increasingly sedentary lifestyle.

A further claim concerns social life. Supporters suggest that when residents spend more time in their own neighbourhood, they are more likely to recognise their neighbours, use local businesses and take part in community activities. Evidence for this effect is, however, largely drawn from surveys of residents' own perceptions, and researchers caution that it is difficult to separate the influence of urban design from that of income, age and length of residence.

Critics raise a number of objections. The most frequently cited is that the model is far easier to apply in dense, historic city centres than in suburbs built around the car, where homes, workplaces and services are often separated by considerable distances. Converting such areas would require substantial investment and, in many cases, changes to planning regulations that have shaped development for decades. Others point out that many jobs cannot be relocated to residential districts, so that a fifteen-minute radius may cover shopping and schooling but not employment.

There are also concerns about fairness. If a neighbourhood becomes more attractive as a result of new parks, cycle lanes and local services, property prices and rents may rise, potentially forcing out the lower-income residents the improvements were intended to benefit. Some housing campaigners therefore argue that any such scheme should be accompanied by measures to protect affordable housing, such as limits on rent increases or a requirement that new developments include a proportion of low-cost homes.

Finally, the concept has attracted opposition from a small number of people who interpret it as an attempt to restrict where residents are allowed to travel. Planners involved in such schemes generally reject this interpretation, stressing that the aim is to make local trips more convenient, not to prevent longer ones. Whatever its eventual impact, the debate illustrates how decisions about the layout of a city can have far-reaching consequences for health, the environment and social equality.

items.prompt: The model aims to bring the different activities of daily life physically closer to people's homes.
items.evidence: the model encourages a mixture of uses within each neighbourhood
items.reason: Work, schools and shops are mixed into residential neighbourhoods, so they are closer to homes.

items.prompt: Supporters believe that the model could remove road traffic problems completely.
items.evidence: even enthusiastic supporters concede that congestion is unlikely to disappear altogether
items.reason: 'Remove completely' is contradicted by 'unlikely to disappear altogether'.

items.prompt: The concept was first put into practice in North America.
items.evidence: European and North American cities are mentioned, but not where the idea was first applied.
items.reason: The passage gives no information about which region used the idea first.

items.prompt: Researchers are confident that the social benefits reported by residents are caused by the design of their neighbourhood.
items.evidence: researchers caution that it is difficult to separate the influence of urban design from that of income, age and length of residence
items.reason: Researchers say the cause is hard to identify, which contradicts 'confident'.

items.prompt: According to some critics, a short walk or cycle from home may not reach the places where many people work.
items.evidence: a fifteen-minute radius may cover shopping and schooling but not employment
items.reason: 'Places where many people work' paraphrases 'employment'.

items.prompt: Summary: Critics argue that the approach suits compact, older city centres better than car-dependent (6) ______.
items.evidence: than in suburbs built around the car
items.reason: 'Car-dependent suburbs' paraphrases 'suburbs built around the car'. Villages are not mentioned, and the critics' contrast is between city centres and suburbs.

items.prompt: Summary: Adapting such areas would be costly and would require new (7) ______.
items.evidence: changes to planning regulations that have shaped development for decades
items.reason: The passage names investment and changes to regulations, not new roads.

items.prompt: Summary: Improving a district could push up housing costs and displace (8) ______ residents.
items.evidence: potentially forcing out the lower-income residents
items.reason: 'Displace poorer residents' paraphrases 'forcing out the lower-income residents'; 'wealthier' is the opposite.

items.prompt: Summary: Some campaigners therefore want safeguards such as caps on (9) ______.
items.evidence: such as limits on rent increases
items.reason: 'Caps on rents' paraphrases 'limits on rent increases'; salaries are not mentioned.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of the final paragraph?
items.evidence: Planners involved in such schemes generally reject this interpretation
items.reason: The paragraph describes a mistaken interpretation, reports the planners' response, and ends with the wider importance of the debate (far-reaching consequences). A is the view the planners reject; B, D are not discussed.
options: A  to argue that the model limits people's freedom to travel
B  to predict that the model will be adopted by most cities
C  to describe a misunderstanding of the concept and stress the wider significance of the debate
D  to compare the views of planners with those of housing campaigners

blocks.title: Speaking Part 3: interactive discussion
blocks.mode: Pair practice in examiner and candidate roles; live feedback from partner and teacher
blocks.instructions: Work in pairs. The examiner asks one question from the list, listens, and then asks one or two follow-up questions. The candidate answers each in three to five sentences: answer, reason, example, and a qualification where it fits. Swap roles after about six minutes.
prompts: Do you think governments should be responsible for making people live more healthily?
How might technology change the way people work over the next twenty years?
What makes a neighbourhood a good place to live?
follow_ups: Why do you think that is?
Could you give me an example?
Would that be true for everyone, or only for some people?
What might be the disadvantages of that?
How might that change in the future?
blocks.routine: Examiner asks a question and one or two follow-ups; candidate develops each answer; after about six minutes, swap. The listener notes one well-developed answer and one place where a precise word would have helped.
blocks.observation: Teacher and partner comment on development (reason, example, qualification) and on vocabulary heard live in the discussion; pronunciation comments are limited to what was heard live.

models.label: Illustrative Part 3 exchange (not a certified band answer)
models.text:
EXAMINER: Do you think governments should be responsible for making people live more healthily?
CANDIDATE: To some extent, yes. Governments can't force people to exercise, but they can make the healthy choice the easy one. For example, if a city builds safe cycle lanes, people who would otherwise drive might cycle to work, which counters the effects of a sedentary lifestyle without anyone being told what to do.
EXAMINER: Would that be true for everyone, or only for some people?
CANDIDATE: Probably not for everyone. Someone with a long commute, or a parent taking three children to school, is unlikely to switch to a bicycle. So I'd say measures like that work best alongside other things, such as better public transport. And there's a cost argument as well: if obesity rates keep rising, it places a strain on health services that everyone pays for, so it's in the government's interest to act early.

blocks.title: Homework: use the collocations in new contexts
blocks.mode: Homework; checked at the start of the next lesson
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-3: Complete each sentence with ONE word. Questions 4-6: Rewrite each sentence using the word-bank item in brackets. Keep the meaning the same.

items.prompt: Online banking has rendered many local bank branches largely ______.
items.evidence: render something obsolete
items.reason: Fixed collocation.

items.prompt: Planting trees along busy streets can ______ the effects of extreme heat.
items.evidence: mitigate the effects of
items.reason: 'Alleviate' is also acceptable with 'the effects of'.

items.prompt: Deforestation has led to widespread habitat ______ in the region.
items.evidence: habitat loss
items.reason: Fixed noun compound.

items.prompt: Rewrite: 'Many workers have jobs with no security and short contracts.' (precarious employment)
items.answer: Many workers are in precarious employment, with short contracts and no job security.
items.evidence: precarious employment
items.reason: Accept any grammatical sentence that uses 'precarious employment' and keeps both ideas (no security, short contracts).

items.prompt: Rewrite: 'Smartphones are making paper maps unnecessary.' (render ... obsolete)
items.answer: Smartphones are rendering paper maps obsolete.
items.evidence: render something obsolete
items.reason: Accept 'have rendered' or 'are rendering'; the object must come between 'render' and 'obsolete'.

items.prompt: Rewrite: 'Group projects help students learn to question ideas and judge evidence.' (foster critical thinking)
items.answer: Group projects foster critical thinking in students.
items.evidence: foster critical thinking
items.reason: Accept any accurate sentence with 'foster critical thinking'; 'among students' or 'in students' are both fine.

blocks.title: Homework: one developed Task 2 body paragraph
blocks.mode: Homework under declared conditions; teacher feedback uses the four criteria
blocks.prompt: Some people believe that the best way to improve public health is to increase the number of sports facilities. Others think this would have little effect and that other measures are needed. Write ONE body paragraph (about 150 words) explaining which other measures you think would be more effective, and why.
blocks.conditions: 20 minutes, in one sitting, without a dictionary, translator or AI tool. Write the start and finish time.
blocks.support: Plan: topic sentence (your main measure) / reason / specific example / qualification or counter-point / link back to the question.
blocks.extension: Include one sentence that concedes a point ('Admittedly, ...') before you return to your argument.
blocks.high_band: Use three word-bank items accurately without forcing them; every sentence should move the argument forward.
blocks.model_label: Illustrative model for teacher feedback only. Not a certified band answer.
blocks.model: In my view, building more sports centres would do little on its own, because the main obstacle for most people is not a lack of facilities but a lack of time and habit. A more effective approach would be to make physical activity part of everyday routines. For instance, cities could invest in safe cycle lanes and wide pavements so that walking or cycling to work becomes the most convenient option, which would counter the effects of a sedentary lifestyle without requiring any extra free time. Admittedly, such changes are expensive and take years to complete. However, they would also alleviate traffic congestion and curb carbon emissions, so the investment would bring several benefits at once. In the long term, measures that change daily behaviour are likely to have more far-reaching consequences for public health than new facilities that only already-motivated people choose to use.
checklist: Task Response: Does the paragraph answer the question (other measures, and why) with a clear position?
Coherence and Cohesion: Does it move from topic sentence to reason, example, concession and conclusion?
Lexical Resource: Are collocations accurate (verb + noun + preposition) and used only where they fit?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Are complex sentences accurate (because, so that, which, although)?

exit_ticket: Two collocations I can now use accurately, with the verb or preposition that goes with them:
One distractor that tricked me today and why it was wrong:
One follow-up question I found hard to answer, and what I would add next time:
homework: Complete the collocation and rewriting tasks on the homework sheet.
Write the body paragraph under timed conditions (20 minutes) and bring it to the next lesson.
delayed_followup: In Lesson 22 (timed essay and long turn), note whether learners use topic collocations accurately and develop Part 3 answers after follow-ups. Record it as a later observation.
mapping_notes: Focuses use Diagnostic Bible section 7.2 construct names where they apply (lexical resource, paraphrase recognition). Teaching focuses only. This optional vocabulary lesson sits outside the 24-lesson sequence and changes no scoring, screener, readiness or band logic.

followup.status: WITHHELD from students until the planned fresh check; approved with lesson v1.1.0 on 2026-10-26. Keep private until use.
followup.delivery: About one teaching week later: 10 minutes, unseen text, no word bank or dictionary. Record timing and support.
followup.review: Score each answer independently. For multiple choice, ask the learner to name why one distractor is wrong. Do not convert to an IELTS band.

blocks.title: Fresh check: which word fits exactly?
blocks.instructions: Choose the correct option, A, B, C or D, to complete each sentence. All the options are real English words.

items.prompt: Rising temperatures are likely to ______ water shortages in the region.
items.evidence: exacerbate a problem = make it worse
items.reason: 'Mitigate' and 'alleviate' mean the opposite; 'deteriorate' cannot take an object (things deteriorate; you cannot deteriorate something).

items.prompt: This rare turtle is classified as an ______ species, so catching it is illegal.
items.evidence: an endangered species
items.reason: An extinct species no longer exists, so it could not be caught; 'extinguished' is used for fires and hopes; a 'dangerous' species would not explain why catching it is illegal.

items.prompt: Uncontrolled urban ______ has pushed the edge of the city twenty kilometres into the countryside.
items.evidence: urban sprawl = uncontrolled outward growth
items.reason: 'Urban extension' is a planning term for planned growth, which contradicts 'uncontrolled'; 'urban stretch' and 'urban spill' are not used.

items.prompt: Cheap air travel has had ______ consequences for the tourism industry.
items.evidence: far-reaching consequences = wide and strong effects
items.reason: 'Far-away' and 'far-off' describe distance; 'far-fetched' means unlikely to be true.

blocks.title: Fresh check: working from home
blocks.instructions: Do the statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

stimulus.title: Working from home
paragraphs: Since the pandemic, a substantial proportion of office employees in many countries have continued to work from home for at least part of the week. Employers who resisted the change at first have discovered that it allows them to recruit from a much wider area and, in some cases, to rent smaller offices. For employees, the most frequently reported benefit is the time saved by not commuting, which many use to strike a better balance between paid work and family responsibilities.

The arrangement is not without drawbacks. Managers in several surveys reported that newly recruited staff found it harder to acquire practical skills when they could not observe experienced colleagues at work. Some workers also described a sense of isolation, and a minority said that the boundary between working hours and personal time had become harder to maintain. Researchers note, however, that these problems were reported far less often by employees who spent two or three days a week in the office than by those who worked remotely all the time.

items.prompt: Employers can now hire people who live further away from the workplace.
items.evidence: allows them to recruit from a much wider area
items.reason: 'Hire people who live further away' paraphrases 'recruit from a much wider area'.

items.prompt: Most employees said that working from home had damaged their family life.
items.evidence: which many use to strike a better balance between paid work and family responsibilities
items.reason: Many report a better balance with family responsibilities; only a minority mention blurred boundaries.

items.prompt: Employees who combined office and home working reported fewer difficulties than full-time remote workers.
items.evidence: these problems were reported far less often by employees who spent two or three days a week in the office
items.reason: 'Combined office and home working' paraphrases 'two or three days a week in the office'.

items.prompt: Working from home has reduced the salaries of most office employees.
items.evidence: Pay is not mentioned in the passage.
items.reason: The passage discusses recruitment, office space, commuting, skills and isolation, but not salaries.
